column1: What is the random-access time for an array element when the index is known?
column2: O(1), because the address is computed from the base address and element offset.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: Why can inserting at the front of an array be O(n)?
column2: Existing elements may need to shift one position to make room, touching a linear number of elements.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What is the amortized append time for a dynamically resized array?
column2: O(1) amortized. Most appends are constant time; an occasional resize copies O(n) elements, but the cost is spread across many appends.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What invariant must a binary search input satisfy?
column2: The search range must be ordered according to the comparison predicate; otherwise discarding half the range is not justified.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What is the time complexity of binary search?
column2: O(log n) comparisons on a sorted random-access sequence, assuming the midpoint and access to each tested element are O(1).
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What is the expected lookup time in a well-sized hash table?
column2: O(1) expected or average time under a suitable hash function and bounded load factor; worst-case lookup can be O(n).
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What is a hash collision?
column2: Two distinct keys map to the same table index. The table must resolve collisions, commonly by chaining or open addressing.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: Why does a hash table resize?
column2: To keep the load factor within a target range so collisions remain manageable and expected operations stay near O(1).
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: Compare separate chaining with open addressing.
column2: Chaining stores collision groups in buckets or linked structures; open addressing stores entries in the table and probes for another slot. Open addressing needs a deletion strategy such as tombstones.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: When is inserting after a known linked-list node O(1)?
column2: When the node reference is already available: update a constant number of pointers. Finding the node first may still cost O(n).
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: Why is random access slow in a linked list?
column2: Nodes are not contiguous and do not provide an index-to-address calculation, so reaching position i generally requires walking from an endpoint: O(n).
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: How can you reverse a singly linked list in O(n) time and O(1) extra space?
column2: Walk through the list while maintaining previous, current, and next pointers; reverse current.next to previous, then advance all pointers.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What does Floyd's tortoise-and-hare algorithm detect?
column2: A cycle in a linked structure. A slow pointer advances one step and a fast pointer two; if they meet, a cycle exists.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What is the defining access rule of a stack?
column2: LIFO: last in, first out. Push and pop happen at the same end, usually in O(1).
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What is the defining access rule of a queue?
column2: FIFO: first in, first out. Enqueue at one end and dequeue at the other, usually in O(1) with a proper implementation.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: Why is a queue implemented with a two-ended linked list or ring buffer instead of removing index 0 from an array?
column2: Removing index 0 from a plain array shifts remaining elements and costs O(n); a deque or ring buffer can maintain both ends in O(1).
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What is a monotonic stack useful for?
column2: It solves next-greater/next-smaller and related range queries in O(n) by maintaining elements in monotonic order and popping each item at most once.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What is the invariant of a binary search tree?
column2: For each node, keys in the left subtree compare smaller and keys in the right subtree compare larger, according to the tree's duplicate policy.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What is the search complexity in a BST of height h?
column2: O(h). It is O(log n) when the tree is balanced and can degrade to O(n) when it becomes a chain.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What property makes a tree height-balanced?
column2: Its height is kept logarithmic in the number of nodes, typically by enforcing a balance invariant such as AVL height differences or red-black coloring rules.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What does an inorder traversal of a BST produce?
column2: Keys in sorted order, assuming the traversal visits left subtree, node, then right subtree and the BST invariant holds.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What is the max-heap invariant?
column2: Every parent key is greater than or equal to its children, so the maximum element is at the root.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What are the typical complexities of binary-heap insert and extract-min/max?
column2: Both are O(log n), because an element may move along the heap height. Reading the root is O(1).
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: Why is a binary heap a natural implementation for a priority queue?
column2: It provides constant-time access to the highest- or lowest-priority item and logarithmic insertion/removal while using a compact array representation.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What is the time complexity of bottom-up heap construction?
column2: O(n), not O(n log n), because most nodes are near the leaves and require little sift-down work.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What is merge sort's time and extra-space complexity?
column2: O(n log n) time in best, average, and worst cases; the usual array implementation uses O(n) auxiliary space.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What is quicksort's average and worst-case complexity?
column2: Average O(n log n); worst-case O(n) when partitions are repeatedly very unbalanced. Randomized or careful pivots reduce the likelihood of the worst case.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What does it mean for a sorting algorithm to be stable?
column2: Equal-key records preserve their original relative order. Stability matters when sorting by multiple keys in successive passes.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: When is counting sort appropriate?
column2: When keys are integers in a manageable bounded range. It can run in O(n + k), but space and time depend on the key range k, not only the number of items.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What is the time complexity of BFS or DFS using adjacency lists?
column2: O(V + E), because each reachable vertex and edge is processed a constant number of times.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: When should you use BFS for shortest paths?
column2: For an unweighted graph, or when every edge has equal cost. BFS explores by distance layers and returns minimum edge-count distance.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What restriction does Dijkstra's algorithm require?
column2: Edge weights must be nonnegative. A negative edge can invalidate the assumption that a finalized distance is optimal.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: When is Bellman-Ford preferred over Dijkstra?
column2: When negative edge weights may exist or when detecting a reachable negative cycle is required; its standard complexity is O(VE).
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What is a topological ordering?
column2: A linear ordering of a directed acyclic graph in which every directed edge u→v places u before v. It exists only for DAGs.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: How does Kahn's topological-sort algorithm detect a cycle?
column2: It repeatedly removes zero-indegree vertices. If fewer than V vertices are removed, the remaining graph contains a directed cycle.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: Compare an adjacency list with an adjacency matrix.
column2: Lists use O(V + E) space and are efficient for sparse graphs; matrices use O(V²) space but provide O(1) edge-existence lookup.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What operations does disjoint-set union support?
column2: Find identifies a set representative; union merges two sets. With path compression and union by rank/size, sequences run in near-constant amortized time O(α(n)).
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: How does Kruskal's algorithm use union-find?
column2: It processes edges in increasing weight order and adds an edge when its endpoints are in different components, using find/union to avoid cycles.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What data structures make an LRU cache O(1) for get and put?
column2: A hash map from key to node plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency. The map finds nodes and the list moves/removes them in O(1).
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What is a trie good for?
column2: Prefix queries over strings. Insert, lookup, and prefix traversal take O(L) time in the key length L, with space depending on stored nodes and alphabet representation.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What is the sliding-window pattern?
column2: Maintain a contiguous interval and move its left/right boundaries while preserving a condition, often reducing a nested scan to O(n).
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: When is a prefix-sum array useful?
column2: For repeated range-sum queries: after O(n) preprocessing, a range sum can be answered in O(1) with two prefix values, subject to the chosen endpoint convention.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What invariant should a two-pointer solution state?
column2: It should state what the current window or pair represents and why moving a pointer cannot discard a valid solution under the problem's ordering/monotonicity assumptions.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What is the difference between worst-case and amortized complexity?
column2: Worst-case bounds one operation; amortized analysis bounds the average cost over a sequence, without assuming random input.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: Why must recursive space include the call stack?
column2: Each active call stores parameters, locals, and return state. A recursion depth of h contributes O(h) stack space even if the algorithm allocates no explicit collection.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What is the purpose of stating an invariant in an interview solution?
column2: An invariant is a condition preserved after each iteration or operation; it makes correctness reasoning and boundary-case debugging explicit.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.

column1: What should you clarify before giving a complexity claim?
column2: Input size and representation, operation semantics, expected versus worst-case assumptions, recursion/auxiliary space, and whether preprocessing is included.
column3: Interview note: state the invariant, boundary assumptions, and why the complexity follows; do not give only the Big-O label.
